title: I'm going to school
goal: Talk about getting around, and meet a distinction English doesn't make: two verbs for "go" — one for a trip happening now, one for habits.
bekal: tell *ísť* from *chodiť* and pick the right one without stopping to think
name a destination with *do*, *na*, or *k*, depending on the kind of place
name means of transport and ask about schedules

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ako sa dostanem do Košíc?
dialogs.intro: Budi is planning to visit Košice this weekend. He asks Eva in class.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Eva, ako sa dostanem do Košíc?
lines.id: Eva, how do I get to Košice?
lines.literal: Eva, how self I-will-get to Košice-gen?

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: You can take the train or the bus.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Vlak. Ide päť a pol hodiny.

notes: **Idem and chodím are two different verbs, not two forms.** *Idem tento piatok* = I'm going this Friday, one specific trip. *Chodím raz za mesiac* = I go once a month, a repeated habit. English uses the same verb for both and leaves the difference to the adverbs; Slovak changes the verb.

**Vlakom, autobusom, električkou** — the vehicle goes in the **instrumental**, with no preposition at all. Literally "by-train", but no word for "by" is written; the ending already says it. The full case comes in unit 17; for now, learn these forms as chunks.

**Do Košíc** uses the genitive plural, because *Košice* is a plural name — like *Athens* in English. Several Slovak towns are plural: *Košice, Piešťany, Levice, Michalovce*. They always take a plural verb: *Košice **sú** krásne*.
**Ide päť hodín** — the verb *ísť* is also used for how long a trip takes and for vehicles that run: *vlak ide*, *autobus ide*, *film ide* (the film is showing). Same verb, four jobs.

**Pôjdeme** is the future of *ísť* — and it's irregular: not *budeme ísť* but *pôjdem, pôjdeš, pôjde, pôjdeme, pôjdete, pôjdu*. It's the only imperfective verb with its own future form. Learn it separately; you'll use it every day.

grammars.title: Ísť or chodiť — once or repeatedly
body: Slovak has two verbs for almost every kind of movement. One describes a single trip that is happening or about to happen; the other describes a habit, or the ability to move in general.
after: **How to choose in two seconds: ask "once or often?"** *Teraz idem do školy* (I'm on my way to school now — once). *Každý deň chodím do školy* (I go to school every day — repeatedly). The time word in the sentence almost always gives you the answer.
**Chodiť also means "can walk"** and "attend regularly": *Dieťa už chodí* (the child can walk now), *Chodím na hodiny slovenčiny* (I take Slovak classes). It's much broader than just "go often".

**For beginners, this mistake won't block understanding** — Slovaks will still get you. But choosing correctly is one of the quickest signs that someone is really learning the language, because you can't guess it from any other language you may know.

grammars.title: Do, na, or k — three ways to say "to"
body: All three mean "to", and each one forces a different case. Luckily the choice follows the pattern you learned in unit 6: places that take *v* take *do*, places that take *na* keep *na*.
after: **The rule that covers almost everything: pair it with the "at" form.** If you know *v škole*, you know *do školy*. If you know *na pošte*, you know *na poštu*. You're not learning a new list — you're using the unit 6 list from the other direction.

**K is for people, not places.** *Idem k lekárovi* (I'm going to the doctor), *idem k Eve* (I'm going to Eva's). To say "at someone's place", Slovak uses *u* + genitive: *som u lekára*, *bývam u brata*.

**Notice that *na* + accusative means motion, *na* + locative means rest.** One preposition, two cases, two meanings. It's the same pattern as *doprava/vpravo* in unit 6 — Slovak separates motion from rest wherever it can.

blocks.text: The third column is the form you'll actually use — instrumental, no preposition. Learn that column directly; the basic form rarely shows up in travel sentences.

Two exceptions: the **bicycle** takes *na bicykli* (on the bike, locative), not the instrumental — because you sit **on** it, not **in** it. And **on foot** is *pešo*, a fixed word that never changes. The same goes for *na koni* (on horseback) and *na motorke* (by motorbike).

blocks.title: Bratislava without a metro
items: Bratislava is one of the few European capitals without a metro — construction began in the 1980s and was then stopped, and the tunnels are still underground. People use the *električka* (tram), the *trolejbus*, and the *autobus*.

Buy your ticket before boarding, and you **must validate it** in the yellow machine inside the vehicle. An unvalidated ticket counts as no ticket, and inspectors (*revízor*) wear plain clothes. The fine is fifty euros — far more than this book.

blocks.text: **Vystupujete?** is a phrase you must recognize on a crowded tram. The person behind you asks it to find out whether they need to squeeze past. The answer is *áno* or *nie*, and it's not small talk — it's a hint that you should move aside if the answer is no.

blocks.title: Free trains for students
items: Students under 26 who are enrolled in Slovakia — including international students — ride domestic trains **for free**; you just register at a station ticket office.
If you're living in Slovakia to study, that's reason enough to visit the *hlavná stanica* in your first week. Bring your passport and a letter from your school.
